summary: Describes using keyed MD5 with the IP Authentication Header to authenticate packets. It was standards-track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1828 specifies how to calculate keyed MD5 authentication data for an IP datagram. The shared key and selected datagram fields are inputs to the calculation, and the result is carried in AH.

subtitle: A keyed MD5 calculation for authenticating IP datagrams with AH.

tldr.problem: IP datagrams need an integrity and authentication check that can be carried in the IP Authentication Header.
tldr.mechanism: The sender combines a shared secret key, the invariant fields of the datagram and the key again, then calculates a 128-bit MD5 digest for the Authentication Data field.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1828 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. The RFC itself describes keyed MD5 for use with the IP Authentication Header.

today: RFC 1828 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. It specifies keyed MD5 for the IP Authentication Header; the RFC's security discussion describes the concerns known when it was written.

sections.title: Keyed MD5 with the Authentication Header
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. RFC 1828 specifies how AH uses a shared key with the MD5 message-digest algorithm.

The shared key should be a cryptographically strong random value, not a guessable string. Implementations must support keys up to 128 bits, and longer keys are encouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: AH carries data that lets a receiver check an IP datagram's integrity and origin. This RFC defines the keyed MD5 calculation used to produce that data.

sections.title: How the Digest Is Calculated
sections.content:
The authenticated input is formed from the key, padding, the datagram and the original key again. Before calculation, the key is filled to the next 512-bit boundary using MD5's padding method.

The datagram's invariant fields are included and variant fields are set to zero. MD5 produces a 128-bit digest, which is placed in the AH Authentication Data field.
sections.plainLanguage: The calculation combines the shared key with the datagram and applies MD5. The resulting 128-bit value is placed in AH for the receiver to check.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says software implementations of MD5 were adequate for commonly deployed LAN and WAN links at the time, but reports that they were too slow for newer link technologies.

The memo asks for suggestions for authentication algorithms with higher throughput that are not patent-encumbered and retain adequate cryptographic strength.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors report that MD5 speed was adequate for common links of the time but may not suit faster link technologies. They invite suggestions for faster alternatives.

sections.title: Security Considerations at Publication
sections.content:
The RFC says the protection depends on MD5, a correct implementation, secure key management and a strong key. It notes that collisions in the MD5 compression function were known, while stating that no practical method to use those collisions against keyed MD5 was then known.

The document also describes a proposed machine-based collision search and says it was unclear whether that attack applied to keyed MD5. It warns that the 128-bit digest length was being approached by available technology and suggests that applications needing extremely high security might later move to longer digests.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes concerns about MD5 and the security of the shared key. Its discussion reflects the authors' assessment at the time of publication.
